materials-selection-001.question: In Ashby's method of materials selection, the design requirements are organized into function, constraints, objective and free variables. In selecting the material for a bicycle frame, which of these is the objective?
choices: The designer is free to choose the outer diameter and wall thickness of the frame tubes
The frame must not yield under the loads in service and must always meet a specified bending stiffness
Make the mass of the frame as small as possible while meeting the required stiffness and strength
materials-selection-001.explanation: Ashby's method first divides the design requirements into four parts. The function is what the component does (such as a beam carrying a load), the constraints are conditions that must be met, the objective is the quantity to be maximized or minimized, and the free variables are dimensions and the like that the designer may vary. “Make the mass as small as possible” is a quantity to minimize, so it is the objective, and the performance index used to rank materials is derived from it. “Must not yield” and “must meet a specified stiffness” are constraints that draw a pass/fail line and are used in the screening stage to eliminate materials that fail them. The outer diameter and wall thickness of the tubes are free variables; eliminating them with the constraint equations leaves the performance index, a combination of material properties only.

materials-selection-002.question: A tie (tension member) of fixed length L must carry a tensile load F without yielding, and its cross-sectional area may be chosen freely. To make it as light as possible, which performance index should be maximized, with σf the yield strength and ρ the density of the material?
materials-selection-002.explanation: The condition for not yielding is F/A ≤ σf, so the required area is A = F/σf. The mass of the tie is m = ρAL = FL(ρ/σf), and since F and L are fixed, minimizing mass means choosing the material with the largest σf/ρ (specific strength). E/ρ (specific modulus) is the index to maximize for a tie whose constraint is not strength but the amount of extension, that is, stiffness. ∛(σf²)/ρ is the index for a beam in bending whose cross-section size is varied to avoid yielding; it comes from the bending stress varying inversely with the cube of the section dimension. The key point is that even for “light and strong,” the index changes with how the load is applied.

materials-selection-003.question: A beam of square cross section with fixed length and bending stiffness is to be made as light as possible by freely varying the size of the cross section. Which performance index should be maximized, with E the Young's modulus and ρ the density?
materials-selection-003.explanation: The deflection of a beam is inversely proportional to the flexural rigidity EI, and the second moment of area of a square section of side b is I = b⁴/12. To meet the specified stiffness, Eb⁴ must be constant, so b² ∝ 1/√E. The mass of the beam is m = ρb²L ∝ ρ/√E, so minimizing mass means choosing the material with the largest √E/ρ. E/ρ is the index for a tie limited by stiffness, used when the cross-sectional area enters directly. ∛E/ρ is for the bending stiffness of a plate (panel) of fixed width whose thickness alone is varied, coming from the stiffness being proportional to the cube of the thickness. In bending, stiffness increases rapidly as the section grows, so low-density materials are favored, which is why wood and CFRP are strong performers as beams.

materials-selection-004.question: On a log–log materials selection chart (Ashby chart) with Young's modulus E on the vertical axis and density ρ on the horizontal axis, what is the slope of the guideline along which the performance index for a light, stiff beam, √E/ρ, is constant?
materials-selection-004.explanation: Setting √E/ρ = C (constant) gives E = C²ρ², and taking logarithms of both sides gives log E = 2 log ρ + 2 log C, a straight line of slope 2. Materials on a line parallel to it perform equally, and the farther the line is shifted toward the upper left, the larger √E/ρ, that is, the lighter a beam of the same stiffness can be made. Slope 1 is the line of constant E/ρ (tie), and slope 3 is the line of constant ∛E/ρ (panel). Slope 1/2 is the mistake of swapping the axes and reading the slope of log ρ = (1/2) log E + constant. On a log–log chart, differences in the exponents of performance indices appear as differences in slope, so a single chart lets you read off the ranking of materials for each loading mode.

materials-selection-005.question: Beams of square cross section designed for the same length and bending stiffness are made of steel (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 g/cm³) and an aluminum alloy (E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.7 g/cm³). If the size of the cross section can be varied freely, about how many times the mass of the steel beam is the mass of the aluminum alloy beam?
materials-selection-005.explanation: The mass of a beam with specified stiffness is proportional to ρ/√E. For the aluminum alloy it is 2.7/√70 = 2.7/8.37 ≈ 0.323, and for steel 7.8/√210 = 7.8/14.5 ≈ 0.538, so the ratio is 0.323/0.538 ≈ 0.60, about 0.60 times. The aluminum alloy beam needs a thicker section because its Young's modulus is one third, but thanks to its low density it is about 40% lighter overall. About 0.35 times looks only at the density ratio (2.7/7.8), ignoring that the section must be thicker to match stiffness. About 1.04 times is the value when mass is proportional to ρ/E, as for a tie in tension; for a tie, aluminum alloy and steel weigh almost the same.

materials-selection-006.question: A tie of fixed length and tensile stiffness is made of steel (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 g/cm³, price per kg taken as 1) and of quasi-isotropic CFRP laminate (E = 70 GPa, ρ = 1.6 g/cm³, price per kg 20 times that of steel). If the cross-sectional area can be varied freely, about how many times the material cost of the steel tie is that of the CFRP tie?
materials-selection-006.explanation: The mass of a stiffness-limited tie is proportional to ρ/E, so the mass ratio CFRP/steel is (1.6/70)/(7.8/210) = 0.0229/0.0371 ≈ 0.62. Material cost is mass times price per kg, so 0.62 × 20 ≈ 12.3, about 12 times. About 0.62 times compares only mass and ignores price. About 20 times looks only at the ratio of prices per kg and ignores that less CFRP mass is needed. When cost is the objective, the performance index becomes E/(Cmρ) (Cm is the price per kg), and CFRP, advantageous in weight, is far worse than steel in material cost. In practice, the decision also includes processing costs and the fuel saved in service by being lighter.

materials-selection-007.question: For a component used at a stress equal to its yield stress σy, the largest crack size that still lets it yield before brittle fracture can be estimated as a = (1/π)(K_IC/σy)² (geometry factor Y = 1). For a steel with σy = 800 MPa and K_IC = 120 MPa·√m, which value is closest to this critical crack length?
materials-selection-007.explanation: K_IC/σy = 120/800 = 0.15 √m, so a = (0.15)²/π = 0.0225/π ≈ 7.2×10⁻³ m, about 7.2 mm. With cracks shorter than this, the whole component yields before fracturing from the crack, so it deforms visibly before it breaks and the problem can be noticed. About 23 mm forgets to divide by π (0.0225 m). About 0.35 mm is what a different high-strength steel (σy = 1500 MPa, K_IC = 50 MPa·√m) would give; in high-strength, low-toughness materials, even small cracks that are hard to find by inspection lead to fracture before yielding. So when fracture must be avoided, materials are selected not by strength alone but with K_IC/σy as the performance index, compared against the crack sizes that inspection can detect.

materials-selection-008.question: For a typical gasoline passenger car, when the energy consumed over the life cycle from material production to disposal is compared stage by stage, which stage is usually the largest, and what materials selection policy follows from it?
choices: The material production stage; using as much material with low embodied energy as possible is most effective
The use (driving) stage; choosing materials that lighten the body and reduce fuel consumption is effective
The disposal stage; it is enough to consider only reducing incineration and landfill
materials-selection-008.explanation: In life cycle assessment (LCA), the use-stage energy from fuel consumed while driving usually accounts for most of the total for a gasoline passenger car. So even aluminum alloys and CFRP, which take a lot of energy to produce, can pay off overall if they lighten the body and improve fuel economy in service. The production stage dominates for products that use no energy in service, such as building materials. The disposal stage generally accounts for a small share of energy, so considering it alone is insufficient. Which stage dominates varies by product, so the basic approach is first to identify it and then choose materials that reduce that stage. The proportions change with the assumptions; in electric vehicles, for example, battery production takes a larger share.

materials-selection-009.question: Take the production energy of aluminum alloy as 200 MJ per kg for primary metal made from ore and 15 MJ per kg for secondary (recycled) metal made by remelting scrap. Which value is closest to the production energy per kg of a material containing 60% secondary metal by mass?
materials-selection-009.explanation: With 40% primary and 60% secondary metal, the weighted average is 0.40 × 200 + 0.60 × 15 = 80 + 9 = 89 MJ/kg. The larger the share of secondary metal, the further the production energy falls below that of primary metal alone. About 108 MJ is the simple average (200 + 15)/2, ignoring the proportions, and about 126 MJ reverses the proportions, 0.60 × 200 + 0.40 × 15. Aluminum uses large amounts of electricity in smelting, while remelting needs less than a tenth of the energy of primary production, so recycling is especially effective for this metal. However, wrought alloys are sensitive to elements mixed in with scrap, so collecting scrap sorted by alloy type is important for maintaining quality.

materials-selection-010.question: When steel scrap is remelted in an electric arc furnace for recycling, which elements tend to accumulate in the steel with repeated recycling and cause problems by degrading quality (tramp elements)?
choices: Copper and tin. They oxidize less readily than iron, so refining cannot remove them, and they cause surface cracking in hot working (hot shortness)
Carbon. Even oxygen-blowing refining cannot remove it, so repeated recycling always turns the steel into a high-carbon steel
Aluminum. It oxidizes less readily than iron, so it does not pass into the slag during refining and stays in the steel
materials-selection-010.explanation: In steel refining, oxygen is blown in to oxidize elements that oxidize more readily than iron, and they are removed as slag. Copper and tin oxidize less readily than iron, so this method cannot remove them; when copper wire from motors and the like gets mixed into scrap, they become more concentrated in the steel with every recycling. During reheating before hot rolling, iron is oxidized preferentially, so copper becomes enriched at the interface with the scale, and above the melting point of copper (about 1085 °C) it becomes liquid, penetrates the grain boundaries and causes cracking. Tin aggravates this. Carbon can be removed as carbon monoxide by oxygen blowing, so the carbon content can be adjusted after recycling. Aluminum oxidizes far more readily than iron and is in fact used as a deoxidizer; it goes into the slag during refining. Tramp elements are controlled by sorting scrap and by dilution with cleaner iron sources.

materials-selection-011.question: Which is an appropriate materials selection and design policy for improving the recyclability of a product?
choices: Bond different kinds of plastics and metals into one piece with adhesives instead of screws to reduce the number of parts, making them impossible to disassemble
Use thermosetting resins, which cannot be melted and reshaped by heat, in as many parts as possible, from the housing to the internal components
Reduce the number of material types, use easily disassembled joints such as screws, and mark plastic parts with their material identification
materials-selection-011.explanation: In recycling, whether collected products can be separated by material strongly affects quality and cost. Reducing the number of material types, using easily removed joints such as screws and snap fits, and marking plastic parts with their material code make dismantling and sorting easier and yield high-purity recycled material. Bonding dissimilar materials into one piece may help reduce weight and part count, but it makes separation difficult and lowers recyclability. Thermosetting resins have a network structure and do not melt when heated, so unlike thermoplastics they cannot be melted and remolded and are difficult to recycle as materials. Performance and recyclability often compete, so both must be compared as objectives.

materials-selection-012.question: You want to minimize two objectives at once, the mass and the cost of a part, but lighter materials are more expensive and no material is best on both. Which is an appropriate way to choose a material in this case?
choices: Choosing the best material on the mass index guarantees it is also the best on cost, so comparing one objective is enough
Collect the Pareto-optimal candidates, which no other candidate beats on both objectives at once, then choose by setting an exchange rate between mass and cost
Add the performance indices for mass (kg) and cost (yen) directly without making the units consistent, and choose the one with the smallest sum
materials-selection-012.explanation: When objectives compete, first pick out the candidates that are not simultaneously beaten on both objectives by any other candidate. These lie on a trade-off curve (the Pareto front), along which improving one objective worsens the other. The final choice is made by deciding an exchange constant, how much money you are willing to pay to save 1 kg, and combining mass and cost into a single evaluation function (penalty function). This is why expensive but light materials are chosen for products where lightness is highly valued, such as aircraft, and cheap materials for ordinary products. The material best for one objective is not necessarily best for the other, so the choice saying the best for one is always the best for the other is wrong. Adding quantities with different units directly makes the result depend on the choice of units, so it is not a meaningful comparison.

materials-selection-013.question: A spring material is to be chosen that stores as much elastic energy per unit volume as possible. The elastic energy per unit volume is σ²/(2E), and the stress σ cannot exceed the failure stress σf of the material. Which performance index should be maximized?
materials-selection-013.explanation: The elastic energy per unit volume is σ²/(2E), and the stress can be at most σf, so the maximum energy that can be stored is σf²/(2E). Dropping the constant 1/2, the index to maximize is σf²/E. High strength counts squared, and a lower Young's modulus lets the material deform more at the same stress and store more energy. Spring steel and rubber are used for springs because this value is large. σf/E is the index for the elastic strain at failure, used to choose parts that must flex a lot without failing, but maximizing energy needs σf squared. E/σf² is the reciprocal of the index, a quantity to be minimized. When comparing per unit mass, σf²/(Eρ), divided further by the density, is used.

materials-selection-014.question: In Ashby's method, candidate materials are narrowed down in two stages, screening and ranking. Which correctly describes how the two stages are used?
choices: Screening removes materials that fail the constraints (such as a minimum service temperature or corrosion resistance), and the rest are ranked by the performance index derived from the objective
Screening by the performance index derived from the objective keeps only the top materials, and the constraints are then converted into scores and added up during ranking
The material with the largest performance index is picked first to fix the ranking, and the design proceeds without checking whether it meets the constraints
materials-selection-014.explanation: Screening applies constraints that must be satisfied for the material to be usable, such as maximum service temperature, corrosion resistance, or electrical insulation, as lower or upper limits on material properties, and removes the materials that fail them. A constraint is either met or not, so it is not converted into a score and added to other properties. Ranking orders the remaining candidates by the performance index derived from the objective (such as minimizing mass or cost). The final choice is then made after looking up detailed information on the top candidates, such as ease of manufacture and service record. Deciding by the performance index alone without checking the constraints risks choosing a material that cannot be used at all, for example one that softens at the service temperature.

materials-selection-015.question: Mass m and cost C of a part are combined into a penalty function Z = αm + C with an exchange constant α = 5000 yen/kg, and the candidate with the smallest Z is chosen. Among candidate A (2.0 kg, 1000 yen), candidate B (1.5 kg, 3000 yen), and candidate C (1.2 kg, 6000 yen), which is chosen?
materials-selection-015.explanation: Computing Z for each: A is 5000 × 2.0 + 1000 = 11000 yen, B is 5000 × 1.5 + 3000 = 10500 yen, and C is 5000 × 1.2 + 6000 = 12000 yen, so B, with the smallest Z, is chosen. The exchange constant α expresses how much one is willing to pay to save 1 kg. The cheapest candidate, A, loses because of its large mass penalty; the lightest, C, loses because its added cost outweighs the value of the mass saved. α varies greatly with the application: with α = 1000 yen/kg, Z is 3000 yen for A, 4500 yen for B, and 7200 yen for C, and the cheapest, A, is chosen. Since the estimate of α decides the choice, it is important to set a value suited to the application.

materials-selection-016.question: A tie of given length and tensile stiffness is to be made as light as possible, with the cross-sectional area free. Comparing steel (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 g/cm³), an aluminum alloy (E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.7 g/cm³) and a titanium alloy (E = 110 GPa, ρ = 4.5 g/cm³), which statement about the result and what it shows is correct?
choices: E/ρ is about 25 GPa·cm³/g for all three, so the tie mass hardly changes; light metals gain in beams and panels
The aluminum alloy has about one third the density of steel, so a tie of equal stiffness also has about one third the mass and is lightest in tension
Steel has the highest Young's modulus and so the highest E/ρ, so a tie of equal stiffness weighs about one third of an aluminum or titanium tie
materials-selection-016.explanation: The mass of a stiffness-limited tie is proportional to ρ/E, so E/ρ is compared. Steel gives 210/7.8 ≈ 26.9, the aluminum alloy 70/2.7 ≈ 25.9 and the titanium alloy 110/4.5 ≈ 24.4 GPa·cm³/g, all about 25. In many metals Young's modulus scales roughly with density, so a member limited by tensile stiffness has almost the same mass whichever metal is used. Low-density metals gain an advantage in beams (√E/ρ) and panels (∛E/ρ), where thickening the section raises stiffness with the square or cube of its size. Taking one third from the density ratio alone forgets that the modulus is also about one third, and choosing steel for its modulus alone ignores the difference in density.

materials-selection-017.question: A beam of given bending stiffness is designed by changing only its size while keeping the shape of its cross-section. Define the shape factor φ as the ratio of the second moment of area to that of a solid round bar of the same area (I = φA²/(4π)); the beam mass is then proportional to ρ/√(φE). Made of the same material as a thin-walled tube with φ = 9, about how many times the mass of a solid round beam (φ = 1) is the beam?
materials-selection-017.explanation: With the same material, ρ and E are unchanged, so the mass ratio is 1/√φ = 1/√9 ≈ 0.33, about 0.33 times. Because a cross-section of area A provides a second moment of area I = φA²/(4π), the required area falls in proportion to 1/√φ. For a thin-walled tube, φ is roughly the ratio of radius to wall thickness r/t, so φ = 9 corresponds to a tube with r/t of about 9. About 0.11 times assumes the mass scales as 1/φ, and about 0.48 times assumes 1/∛φ; neither matches a beam whose stiffness depends on the square of the area. Making the wall too thin causes local buckling, so each material has an upper limit on usable φ, and the performance index is compared in the form √(φE)/ρ.

materials-selection-018.question: A 1.0 m long aluminum alloy tie (E = 70 GPa, σy = 250 MPa, ρ = 2700 kg/m³) carries a tensile load of 10 kN. What is the minimum mass that both avoids yielding and keeps the elongation at or below 1.0 mm? The cross-sectional area can be chosen freely.
materials-selection-018.explanation: The no-yield condition F/A ≤ σy gives A ≥ 1.0×10⁴/(250×10⁶) = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m², a mass of 2700 × 4.0×10⁻⁵ × 1.0 ≈ 0.11 kg. The elongation condition FL/(EA) ≤ 1.0 mm gives A ≥ 1.0×10⁴ × 1.0/(70×10⁹ × 1.0×10⁻³) ≈ 1.43×10⁻⁴ m², a mass of about 0.39 kg. Satisfying both requires the larger area, so the minimum mass is about 0.39 kg, and stiffness is the active (governing) constraint in this design. About 0.11 kg considers strength only and would stretch by about 3.6 mm, breaking the constraint. About 0.49 kg adds the two masses, but the same cross-section satisfies both conditions at once, so they are not added.

materials-selection-019.question: Heat enters one side of a precision instrument component at a constant heat flux, setting up a temperature gradient through its thickness, so the component bends through differential thermal expansion. With the heat flux fixed, which way of choosing the material minimizes this bending (thermal distortion)?
choices: Choose a material with a high κ/α, thermal conductivity divided by expansion coefficient, so both the temperature gradient and the tendency to expand are small
Choose a material with a low thermal conductivity κ, so heat passes poorly through the part and the temperature of the opposite face stays unchanged
Choose a material with a high σf/(Eα), so the thermal stress produced by the temperature difference does not reach the failure stress σf
materials-selection-019.explanation: When a steady heat flux q passes, Fourier's law gives a temperature gradient of q/κ, so the strain gradient through the thickness, that is the curvature of bending, is proportional to αq/κ. With q fixed, the curvature is minimized by making α/κ small, in other words κ/α large; this is the performance index for avoiding thermal distortion. A material with low thermal conductivity makes the temperature gradient larger for the same flux, so the bending actually increases. σf/(Eα) is the index for resisting fracture under thermal stress from sudden temperature changes, a different criterion from the amount of bending, which can occur without cracking. Materials with a high κ/α include silicon and silicon carbide, which conduct heat well and expand little.

materials-selection-020.question: The cost per part is estimated as material cost + tooling cost ÷ number of parts + hourly cost of equipment and labor ÷ parts made per hour. Which is the correct way to compare die casting, which uses an expensive metal die, with sand casting, whose molds are cheap?
choices: Tooling cost is charged equally on every part, so the difference in cost per part does not change with batch size, and the process with cheaper material should be chosen
Tooling cost is divided by the number of parts, so sand casting is cheaper for few parts and die casting for many, swapping at a crossover batch size
The share of tooling cost grows with the number of parts, so sand casting with cheap molds wins in mass production and die casting suits prototypes
materials-selection-020.explanation: Tooling cost is a fixed cost paid once however many parts are made, so per part it is divided by the number made and shrinks as that number grows. Die casting uses an expensive die but has a short cycle time and a low cost per part, so it becomes more favorable as the number of parts rises. If, for example, the tooling costs 100,000 yen for sand molds and 3,000,000 yen for the die, and the other costs per part are 1500 and 300 yen, the crossover is (3,000,000 − 100,000)/(1500 − 300) ≈ 2400 parts. Treating tooling as a per-part cost removes the effect of batch size. Saying the share of tooling cost grows in mass production is backwards; the share falls as the number of parts increases.
